# DbLive — complete reference for AI coding agents

> DbLive is a .NET library that deploys a folder of SQL scripts (migrations, re-runnable code objects, SQL unit tests) to Microsoft SQL Server or PostgreSQL, with a separate "breaking changes" phase for zero-downtime releases, checksum validation and per-database state tracking.
>
> This file is the single source of truth for agents. Every rule below was derived from the DbLive source code (repository https://github.com/zacoders/DbLive, main branch, November 2026). If the installed package behaves differently, the source wins: check `src/DbLive/`.

---

## 0. Read this first: hard rules for agents

Follow these when you create or change files in a DbLive project. Each rule names the failure you cause by breaking it.

1. **Never edit a migration item after it was applied** to any shared database (`<version>.migration.sql`, `<version>.breaking.sql` once deployed). Create a new version instead. Breaking this → `MigrationChecksumMismatchException` on the next deploy (default `MigrationChecksumMode` is `Strict`). Whitespace and comments count; CRLF/LF line endings do not.
2. **Never delete an applied migration version, and never change its version number.** A version that is applied in the database but missing from the project → `DatabaseAheadOfProjectException`, and the deployment changes nothing (Section 5.2).
3. **Code files must be re-runnable.** They are re-executed whenever their content changes and on every new database. Use `create or alter` (SQL Server) or `create or replace` / `drop ... if exists` + `create` (PostgreSQL).
4. **Migrations must be backward compatible (expand only).** Put destructive changes to tables (drop column/table, remove sync triggers) into `<version>.breaking.sql` of the same version; drop an old version of a code object in a breaking script of the Code folder next to its file (`Code/dbo/GetUser.breaking.sql`, Section 6.1). Breaking scripts run only when `DeployBreaking = true`.
5. **Never write undo scripts.** DbLive has none and does not roll back a database: a release is rolled back by rolling back the application before its breaking phase, and a wrong migration is fixed by a new migration (Section 18.8). Breaking this (`<version>.undo.sql`, `<version>.u.sql`, `<version>.undo.settings.json` in `Migrations`) → `UndoNotSupportedException` before anything is deployed.
6. **BeforeDeploy and AfterDeploy scripts run on every deployment** (not once). They must be idempotent: a second run must not fail and must not change the schema.
7. **SQL Server test files must not contain `GO`.** Test scripts are sent as one command. (`GO` is fine in migrations, breaking, code, BeforeDeploy/AfterDeploy and `setup.test.sql`.)
8. **The assertion marker column is named `assert` and must be the first column** of its result set (case does not matter; `select 'rows' as assert` works on both engines). A misspelled name (`asstert`) or a missing alias (`select 'rows'`) → the test fails with "... looks like an assert result set ..." (Section 8.3).
9. **Every build deployed to a database must contain all migrations applied there.** All folders are optional (a code-only project without `Migrations` is valid), but if a database already has applied migrations and the build lacks them (for example, a migration file was deleted, or the deployer was built from an older commit), the deployment fails before any change → `DatabaseAheadOfProjectException`. The same holds for DbLive itself: a build whose DbLive packages are older than the version the database requires fails before any change → `DatabaseRequiresNewerDbLiveException` (Section 15).
10. **The `.csproj` of the SQL project names the scripts root folder, `<DbLiveScriptsFolder>Scripts</DbLiveScriptsFolder>`, and the project references a DbLive package**, which embeds the folder in the assembly (Section 3.1): the provider, `DbLive.xunit`, or `DbLive` itself in a project with only scripts. Name the folder `Scripts` unless the project already uses another name. Do not add an `EmbeddedResource` for the scripts or the `ProjectDir` metadata to the `.csproj`. Breaking this → an `EmbeddedResource` of the scripts next to the property fails the build with "Remove the DbLive block from <project>.csproj" (a leftover `ProjectDir` item does not fail it; remove it too); a SQL project without the property or without a DbLive package reference builds, and `SetProject` throws `ScriptsNotEmbeddedException`. Do not copy scripts to the output folder; DbLive does not read them from there.
11. **Do not create anything in the `dblive` schema.** DbLive owns it (Section 15).
12. **Do not run SQL tests against production.** A deployment never runs them; they run in `dotnet test` against a disposable database (Section 13), and a production deployer does not call `IDbLiveTester.RunAllTestsAsync()` (Section 8.2). Tests run in rolled-back transactions, but with `Serializable` isolation by default, so they take locks on production tables.
13. **Settings files are per script, not per version**: `<version>.migration.settings.json`, `<version>.breaking.settings.json` (short `<version>.m.s.json`, `.b.s.json`), keys `TransactionWrapLevel` (`Migration`|`None`), `TransactionIsolationLevel`, `Timeout` (Section 9.3). The old `<version>.settings.json` → `ObsoleteMigrationSettingsFileException`; the old key `MigrationTimeout` → `InvalidMigrationItemSettingsException`.
14. **Follow the way the project uses DbLive** (Section 1). In a classic project (no `_vN` object names in `Code/`, no breaking scripts) change procedures in place and do not introduce versioned names or breaking scripts unless asked. In a project with a versioned interface: when the **contract** of an interface object changes (new required parameter, other result columns, other meaning), rename the object in the same file to the next version (`MyProc_v1` → `MyProc_v2`) and drop the old version in a breaking script next to the file (`my-proc.breaking.sql` next to `my-proc.sql`, Section 18.6); when only the **implementation** changes, keep the name. Breaking this → running applications that still call the old name fail (missing parameter, changed result set), or a classic project collects versions that nobody drops.
15. **Breaking scripts of the Code folder run on every breaking deployment** (`breaking.sql`, `b.sql`, `*.breaking.sql`, `*.b.sql` under `Code/`; Section 6.1). They must be idempotent: `drop proc if exists`, `drop function if exists`; a second run must not drop more than the first one. Breaking this → the second breaking deployment fails or changes the schema (`[SqlDeployFact]` catches both; a schema change → `SchemaChangedException`). Never give a code object file such a name: it is not deployed as code. A name that also matches `TestFilePatterns` (`test.breaking.sql`, `t.b.sql`) → `BreakingScriptMatchesTestPatternException`.
16. **Put nothing into the scripts root except the project folders and `settings.json`.** Every file must be inside `Migrations`, `Code`, `Tests`, `BeforeDeploy` or `AfterDeploy` (or the folders named in `settings.json`); hidden files and folders (the name starts with a dot: `.DS_Store`, `.gitkeep`) do not count. Breaking this (a `PostDeployment/` folder, a `README.md` or a misspelled `setting.json` in the root) → `FilesOutsideProjectFoldersException` before any script of the project runs (Section 4). Keep other scripts and documents outside the scripts root; notes (`.md`, `.txt`) may sit inside the project folders.
17. **Give every project a `ProjectId`** in `Scripts/settings.json` (Section 14): a name unique to the project, the same in every environment (`"ProjectId": "billing-api-db"`). Breaking this → nothing stops the deployer from deploying into another project's database, and every deployment logs the warning "ProjectId is not set in settings.json ...".
18. **Do not turn on `CreateDbIfNotExists` in a production deployer** (Section 18.10). It is off by default; turn it on only for local and test databases. Breaking this → a typo in the database name of the connection string creates an empty database and deploys the whole schema into it.

---

## 1. What DbLive is and when to use it

- **Migrations**: versioned, ordered, applied once per database. An optional breaking (contract phase) script for each version. No undo scripts: DbLive does not roll back a database (Section 18.8).
- **Code**: stored procedures, functions, views, triggers, schemas. One file per object, re-executed when the file changes. Never dropped automatically.
- **SQL tests**: `.sql` files with Arrange / Act / Assert, each run in a transaction that is always rolled back. They run as individual xUnit tests in Visual Studio / `dotnet test`: a fixture deploys the project into a new database (Docker via Testcontainers, or a local server) and drops it afterwards, so no shared test database is needed (Section 13). A deployment never runs them. Without xUnit v2 (NUnit, MSTest, xUnit v3) or against a database that is already deployed, `RunAllTestsAsync` runs them all with one call (Section 8.2).
- **Breaking phase**: destructive changes run in a separate deployment, after the old application version is gone (zero-downtime expand/contract).
- **Rollback of a release**: the application is rolled back, the database stays: before its breaking phase a release only adds, so the database serves both versions (Section 18.8). Deploying an older build with fewer migrations fails with `DatabaseAheadOfProjectException` and changes nothing (Section 5.2).
- **ProjectId**: binds a project to a database to prevent deploying to the wrong one.
- **No CLI.** You write a small console app (the "deployer") or call DbLive from tests. `src/DbLive.Console` in the repository is an empty stub.

Model DbLive is built around (recommended, not enforced): the database is a separate service with its own interface, release cycle and tests; applications call versioned procedures/functions/views (`GetUsers_v1`, `GetUsers_v2`) and do not query tables directly; migrations reshape tables freely behind that interface. One file holds one interface object and is changed in place; git history is the object's history. Direct table access is possible, but then a table used by applications is part of the interface and is hard to change without downtime.

Ways a project can use DbLive (each adds to the previous one; find out which one the project uses before changing it, rule 14):

| Way | What the project uses | How to recognize it |
|---|---|---|
| Classic | Migrations and code | No breaking scripts, no `_vN` names in `Code/` |
| Zero downtime | Backward-compatible (expand-only) migrations, breaking scripts, scripts without a transaction where needed (Section 10) | `<version>.breaking.sql` files, sync triggers, item settings with `"TransactionWrapLevel": "None"` |
| Database as a service | Plus a versioned interface of procedures/functions | `_v1`/`_v2` (or `Name2`) object names in `Code/`, breaking scripts that drop old versions (`Code/**/*.breaking.sql`, or in migrations in older projects) |

SQL tests, checksums and ProjectId are available in every way.

---

## 2. Packages and requirements

| Package | Purpose | Key API |
|---|---|---|
| `DbLive` | Core engine. Pulled in automatically by the other packages. Embeds the scripts folder that the `.csproj` names in `DbLiveScriptsFolder` in the assembly (Section 3.1). | `DbLiveBuilder`, `DeployParameters`, `IDbLive`, `IDbLiveFixtureBuilder` |
| `DbLive.MSSQL` | SQL Server / Azure SQL provider (Microsoft.Data.SqlClient + SMO). | `.SqlServer()`, `MsSqlFixtureBuilder` |
| `DbLive.PostgreSQL` | PostgreSQL provider (Npgsql). | `.PostgreSQL()`, `PostgreSqlFixtureBuilder` |
| `DbLive.xunit` | xUnit **v2** integration: SQL tests as test cases, deployment tests. | `[SqlFact]`, `[SqlDeployFact]`, `DbLiveTestFixture`, `DeploymentTest` |
| `DbLive.Testcontainers.MSSQL` | Test database: SQL Server in Docker (Testcontainers). Brings `DbLive.MSSQL` and `Testcontainers.MsSql`; no xUnit dependency. | `MsSqlContainerFixtureBuilder` |
| `DbLive.Testcontainers.PostgreSQL` | Test database: PostgreSQL in Docker (Testcontainers). Brings `DbLive.PostgreSQL` and `Testcontainers.PostgreSql`; no xUnit dependency. | `PostgreSqlContainerFixtureBuilder` |
| `DbLive.Templates` | `dotnet new` template; installed with `dotnet new install`, never referenced by a project. Creates a new solution (Section 18.1). | `dotnet new dblive` |

- Versions: all DbLive packages are released together with one version; use the same version of all of them. A project created by `DbLive.Templates` references the DbLive packages of the template's version. Semantic Versioning, breaking changes only in a major version (`docs/versioning.md`). Before upgrading to a new major version, read "Breaking changes" in the release notes (https://github.com/zacoders/DbLive/releases) and apply the upgrade steps there.
- Target frameworks: `net8.0`, `net9.0`, `net10.0`.
- Logging: Serilog (`Serilog.ILogger`). Default is no logging.
- DI: Microsoft.Extensions.DependencyInjection (internal container, all services are singletons).
- The provider package embeds DbLive's own SQL scripts (the `dblive` schema, Section 15) in its assembly as resources named `DbLive.Internal/...`. Nothing is copied next to the application. A `DbLive.MSSQL/` or `DbLive.PostgreSQL/` folder left in `bin/` by an older package version is not read and can be deleted.

```bash
dotnet add package DbLive.MSSQL                  # or: dotnet add package DbLive.PostgreSQL
dotnet add package DbLive.xunit                  # only in the xUnit test project
dotnet add package DbLive.Testcontainers.MSSQL   # only in the test project, for a test database in Docker; or DbLive.Testcontainers.PostgreSQL
dotnet add package DbLive                        # only in a SQL project without the provider (layout B, Section 3.2)
dotnet new install DbLive.Templates              # the template for a new solution (Section 18.1), not a project reference
```

---

## 3. Project setup

### 3.1 How the scripts get into the assembly

The `DbLive` package embeds the scripts. The `.csproj` of the SQL project names their folder, relative to the project, and references a DbLive package:

```xml
<PropertyGroup>
  <DbLiveScriptsFolder>Scripts</DbLiveScriptsFolder>
</PropertyGroup>
```

NuGet imports the package's `buildTransitive/DbLive.props` into every project that has `DbLive` in its graph: a direct `PackageReference`, a provider package, `DbLive.xunit`, or a `ProjectReference` to a project with one of them. A project that sets `DbLiveScriptsFolder` gets these items; do not write them into the `.csproj`:

```xml
<EmbeddedResource Include="Scripts\**\*" LogicalName="DbLive/%(RecursiveDir)%(Filename)%(Extension)" WithCulture="false" />
<AssemblyAttribute Include="System.Reflection.AssemblyMetadata"><_Parameter1>ProjectDir</_Parameter1><_Parameter2>$(ProjectDir)</_Parameter2></AssemblyAttribute>
<AssemblyAttribute Include="System.Reflection.AssemblyMetadata"><_Parameter1>DbLiveScriptsFolder</_Parameter1><_Parameter2>Scripts</_Parameter2></AssemblyAttribute>
```

A project without the property gets nothing, not even the metadata, whatever folders it has: the deployer and the test project of layout B, a test project of the application with its own `Scripts` folder. `DbLiveScriptsFolder` has no default; any folder works (`Db`, `Database/Scripts`). Resource names stay relative to it (`DbLive/Migrations/001.migration.sql`), so the relative paths stored in the database do not depend on the folder name.

- Resource names: every file under the folder becomes `DbLive/<path relative to the folder>`. Only resources starting with `DbLive/` are read; `\` in names (from `%(RecursiveDir)` on Windows) is treated as `/`. A file such as `name.fr.sql` or `name.de-DE.sql` stays in the assembly (`WithCulture="false"`); MSBuild would otherwise treat it as a localized resource and move it to a satellite assembly.
- `ProjectDir` and `DbLiveScriptsFolder` are used only by `[SqlFact]` discovery for "go to source" (Section 13.2).
- A `.csproj` that sets `DbLiveScriptsFolder` and embeds the scripts itself as well (an `EmbeddedResource` with `LogicalName="DbLive/..."`, or any `EmbeddedResource` of the same files) fails the build: "The DbLive package embeds the scripts of the 'Scripts' folder named by <DbLiveScriptsFolder> in the assembly, and <project>.csproj embeds N DbLive script(s) too. Remove the DbLive block from <project>.csproj ...". Remove the `EmbeddedResource` and the `ProjectDir` `AssemblyAttribute`. To embed the scripts in the `.csproj` yourself, leave out `DbLiveScriptsFolder` and write the items above.
- Upgrading a project from a version that copied the scripts to the output folder (1.5.0 and earlier): remove the `ClearOutput` target, the `None` items with `TargetPath` that copy `Scripts`, and the `ProjectDir` `AssemblyAttribute` from the `.csproj`, and add `<DbLiveScriptsFolder>Scripts</DbLiveScriptsFolder>`. A SQL project with only scripts adds a `DbLive` package reference.
- A project that references the DbLive projects from source by `ProjectReference` (not the packages) does not get the file from NuGet; it imports `src/DbLive/buildTransitive/DbLive.props` itself, as the demos do in `src/Demo/Directory.Build.props`, and sets `DbLiveScriptsFolder`.
- Nothing is copied to `bin/`, so there is nothing to clean: a deleted or renamed script is gone from the next build, and projects that reference the SQL project do not get copies of the scripts.
- The scripts are read from the dll with the same relative paths and the same text (UTF-8, BOM detected) as from the folder, so switching an existing database from copied scripts to embedded scripts changes no checksums and redeploys no code.

### 3.2 Layouts

**A. One project** (scripts and deployer together; this is what the demos and `dotnet new dblive` do):

```
MyDb/
  MyDb.csproj          <- OutputType Exe, <DbLiveScriptsFolder>Scripts</DbLiveScriptsFolder>, references DbLive.MSSQL, which embeds Scripts/ (3.1)
  Program.cs           <- deployer
  Scripts/
    settings.json      <- optional
    Migrations/        <- all folders are optional
    Code/
    Tests/
    BeforeDeploy/
    AfterDeploy/
```

**B. Separate projects** (recommended for larger solutions):

```
MyDb/            class library: Scripts/ + an empty marker class; <DbLiveScriptsFolder>Scripts</DbLiveScriptsFolder>, references DbLive, which embeds Scripts/ (3.1)
MyDb.Deploy/     console app: references MyDb and DbLive.MSSQL; Program.cs
MyDb.Tests/      xUnit v2 test project: references MyDb, DbLive.xunit, DbLive.Testcontainers.MSSQL (brings DbLive.MSSQL)
```

Get the SQL project's assembly through a type in it, for example `public sealed class MyDbMarker { }` and `typeof(MyDbMarker).Assembly`. `Assembly.Load("MyDb")` also works when the project is referenced.

### 3.3 Deployer (`Program.cs`)

```csharp
using DbLive;
using DbLive.MSSQL;          // DbLive.PostgreSQL for PostgreSQL
using System.Reflection;

string connectionString = Environment.GetEnvironmentVariable("MYDB_CONNECTION_STRING")
    ?? "Server=localhost;Database=MyDb;Trusted_Connection=True;TrustServerCertificate=True;";

bool breaking = args.Contains("--breaking");

IDbLive deployer = new DbLiveBuilder()
    .LogToConsole()
    .SqlServer()                                   // or .PostgreSQL()
    .SetDbConnection(connectionString)
    .SetProject(Assembly.GetExecutingAssembly())   // layout B: typeof(MyDbMarker).Assembly; reads the scripts embedded in it, see 3.4
    .CreateDeployer();

await deployer.DeployAsync(breaking
    ? DeployParameters.Breaking
    : DeployParameters.Default);
```

An unhandled exception gives a non-zero exit code, so CI steps fail correctly. The deployer does not run the SQL tests: a deployment never runs them, and a production deployer must not (rule 12). They run in the xUnit test project (Section 13); do not add `RunAllTestsAsync()` to the deployer.

`DeployParameters.Default` does not create the database (`CreateDbIfNotExists` is off), so the database must exist; otherwise `DatabaseNotFoundException`. For a local or test database deploy with `DeployParameters.Default with { CreateDbIfNotExists = true }`; never in a production deployer (rule 18).

### 3.4 Where DbLive reads scripts from (`SetProject`, `SetScriptsFolder`)

| Call | Scripts are read from | Typical use |
|---|---|---|
| `SetProject(Assembly projectAssembly)` | the resources of `projectAssembly` named `DbLive/...` (Section 3.1) | Deployers and test projects |
| `SetScriptsFolder(string scriptsPath)` | the folder; a relative path is resolved against the current directory | Scripts that are not built into an assembly |

Notes:
- `SetProject` does not depend on the current working directory or on files next to the application: the dll you build is what gets deployed, also after `dotnet publish` or in a Docker image. A script change needs a build; Visual Studio, `dotnet run` and `dotnet test` build first.
- Test projects reference the SQL project and call `SetProject` with its assembly, so they deploy and test the same scripts as the deployer.
- `SetProject` throws `ScriptsNotEmbeddedException` (it names the assembly and lists what to check: `DbLiveScriptsFolder` in the `.csproj`, a DbLive package reference, the folder) when the assembly has no `DbLive/` resources, instead of deploying an empty project. A provider assembly (`DbLive.MSSQL`, `DbLive.PostgreSQL`) passed by mistake throws it too: its own scripts are named `DbLive.Internal/...`.
- `SetScriptsFolder` throws `DirectoryNotFoundException` when the folder does not exist. A builder reads the project once, on first use: the list of files, each file and `settings.json`. A later deployment from the same builder does not see files added, deleted or changed since; create a new builder for each build to deploy. A failed read is not kept: after an I/O error (a file locked for a moment by an antivirus or an editor) the next deployment from the same builder reads that file or `settings.json` again.
- Both calls give the same scripts: DbLive works only with relative paths (`Migrations/001.migration.sql`, `/` on every OS). Logs, exception messages and Test Explorer show them with the real names of the files and folders, not the casing of the folder names in `settings.json`; only the log of code files removed from the project shows the stored lower-case paths (Section 15). The database stores them in lower case (Section 15), so a file is identified ignoring case; two files whose paths differ only by case fail the deployment (Section 4). After `Starting deployment.` and the deployment of DbLive's own schema, the log names the source: `Starting project deploy from MyDb.dll.` or the folder path.
- "Go to source" of `[SqlFact]` tests does not depend on these calls: discovery reads the `ProjectDir` and `DbLiveScriptsFolder` metadata of the fixture builder's assembly (Section 13.2).

---

## 4. Scripts folder: discovery rules

Paths below are relative to the scripts root. Folder names are configurable in `settings.json` (Section 9), also as nested paths written with `/` or `\` (both work on any OS).

| Folder (default name) | Required | Files picked up | Search | Order |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `Migrations` | no | `*.sql`, `*.json`; any subfolder | recursive | by version number |
| `Code` | no | `*.sql` except files matching `TestFilePatterns`, breaking scripts and `setup.test.sql` | recursive | groups from `CodeSubFoldersDeploymentOrder` first, then the rest; inside a group the files start by relative path, run in parallel with retries |
| `Code` (breaking scripts) | no | `breaking.sql`, `b.sql`, `*.breaking.sql`, `*.b.sql` (Section 6.1) | recursive | by relative path; only in the breaking phase |
| `Tests` | no | every `*.sql` except `setup.test.sql` | each folder, all subfolders | parallel |
| `Code` (tests) | no | files matching `TestFilePatterns` (default `test.*.sql`, `t.*.sql`, `*.test.sql`, `*.t.sql`) except `setup.test.sql` | each folder, all subfolders | parallel |
| `BeforeDeploy` | no | `*.sql` | recursive | by relative path |
| `AfterDeploy` | no | `*.sql` | recursive | by relative path |
| root | no | `settings.json` | root only | — |

A missing folder is skipped. A project without `Migrations` deploys only code and BeforeDeploy/AfterDeploy scripts, and its tests run as usual (Section 8); rule 9 in Section 0 still applies.

Nothing else may be in the scripts root. A file outside the five project folders (the names from `settings.json`, also nested ones such as `db/Code`) that is not `settings.json` in the root fails the deployment with `FilesOutsideProjectFoldersException`: DbLive would never read it, so a `PostDeployment/` folder would never run and a misspelled `setting.json` would leave every setting at its default. The exception gives the number of such files, names the first five by relative path, and lists the project folders. The check runs on every read of the project, like the case check below, so the deployment stops when it loads the project (Section 12, step 1), before it changes anything on the server; `[SqlFact]` discovery and `IDbLiveTester` fail the same way. Hidden files and folders, whose name starts with a dot (`.DS_Store`, `.gitkeep`, `.vs/`), do not count as outside. Inside a project folder they are read like any other file: `Code/.old/x.sql` is deployed, and a macOS `Migrations/._001.migration.sql` fails with `InvalidMigrationVersionException`. There is no setting to allow other folders: keep such files outside the scripts root (for `SetProject`, outside the `Scripts` folder that the DbLive package embeds). With `CodeFolder: ""` every file is in the Code folder, so the check never fails.

Folders, file patterns, `settings.json` and the parts of a migration file name, extension included (`001.Migration.SQL`, Section 5.1), are matched ignoring case on every OS and in every culture (`001.BREAKING.sql` is a breaking script also in `tr-TR`). "By relative path" means ordinal, ignoring case (`StringComparer.OrdinalIgnoreCase` on the path with `/`), the same on every OS and in every culture: `a-b/x.sql`, `A.sql`, `a/x.sql`, `a_b.sql`, `b.sql`.

Two files whose relative paths differ only by case (`Code/dbo/GetUser.sql` and `Code/dbo/getuser.sql`, or `Tests/Orders/x.sql` and `Tests/orders/x.sql`; possible only on a case-sensitive file system such as Linux) fail the deployment with `ScriptPathsDifferOnlyByCaseException`, which names both paths. The check covers every file of the project, whatever its folder or extension (also ignored `.txt`/`.md` files), and runs on every read of the project, so a deployment stops when it loads the project (Section 12, step 1), before it changes anything on the server; `[SqlFact]` discovery and `IDbLiveTester` fail the same way. Reason: DbLive finds files and identifies them in `dblive` ignoring case (Section 15), so such files would be one item. Never create two files whose paths differ only by case; rename or delete one of them.

Other files (`.txt`, `.md`, ...) inside the project folders are ignored, except in `Migrations`: a `.json` file there that is not an item settings file `<version>.<item>.settings.json` (Section 5.1) fails the deployment (`UnknownMigrationSettingsException`; the old `<version>.settings.json` / `<version>.s.json` → `ObsoleteMigrationSettingsFileException`), and so does a `.sql` or `.json` file whose name does not start with a version number (`config.json`, `readme.sql` → `InvalidMigrationVersionException`). A `.txt` in `Migrations` is ignored (the demos keep `002.notes.txt` next to migrations).

Encoding: every file DbLive reads (scripts, item settings files, `settings.json`) is UTF-8, with or without a BOM; UTF-16 and UTF-32 are read only with a BOM (SSMS saves UTF-16 LE with a BOM, which works). The same rule holds for `SetProject` and `SetScriptsFolder`. A file with bytes that are not UTF-8, such as a script saved in Windows-1252 or Windows-1251 without a BOM (the ANSI code page of an old editor), fails with `FileNotUtf8Exception`, which names the file (`RelativePath`) and where it was read from (the folder or the dll). Reason: read as UTF-8, each of its non-ASCII characters would become `U+FFFD` (`�`) and be deployed so, in comments and in string literals alike (`N'Résumé'` → `N'R�sum�'` in the table); DbLive 1.x did that without an error. The files the deployment runs and `settings.json` are read when the project is loaded (Section 12, step 1), so the deployment stops before it changes anything on the server; a test file fails when the tests are read (`[SqlFact]` discovery, `IDbLiveTester`). There is no setting for another encoding and no detection of it: the same file would give another text and another checksum on another machine. Save the file as UTF-8; for a migration or breaking script that is already applied, see Section 18.2, because converting it changes its checksum. Two cases are not caught: a UTF-8 BOM followed by bytes of another encoding is read with `U+FFFD`, and UTF-16 without a BOM is read as UTF-8 with `\0` characters when its text is ASCII or Cyrillic. Always write files of a DbLive project in UTF-8.

`setup.test.sql` is the test setup file of its folder (Section 8.1), in `Tests/` and in `Code/`. It is never a test and never deployed as code, whatever `TestFilePatterns` contains. The name is fixed: an `init.sql` (the old name) is a test in `Tests/` and a code object in `Code/`.

A file of `Code/` named like a breaking script (`breaking.sql`, `b.sql`, `*.breaking.sql`, `*.b.sql`, ignoring case) is never a code item and never a test. If its name also matches `TestFilePatterns` (with the defaults: `test.breaking.sql`, `t.b.sql`, `test.b.sql`, `t.breaking.sql`), every read of the project fails with `BreakingScriptMatchesTestPatternException`, which names the file, so the deployment stops when it loads the project (Section 12, step 1), before it changes anything on the server. The breaking names apply only in `Code/`: `Tests/b.sql` is a test, `Migrations/001.b.sql` is the breaking script of version 1.

---

## 5. Migrations

### 5.1 File name grammar

```
<version>.<type>.<name>.sql                    script with explicit type
<version>.<name>.sql                           no type -> Migration
<version>.<type>.<settings>[.<name>].json      settings of the <type> script of that version
```

- `<version>`: the first dot-separated part, digits only, parsed as a 64-bit integer (`long`) the same way in every culture. `001`, `1`, `20260808104925` are valid; a sign or a space (`+001`, `-5`, ` 001`) is not. `001` and `1` are the **same** version.
- `<type>` (case-insensitive):

| Type token | Item type | `.sql` file | `.json` file (`<settings>` = `settings` or `s`) |
|---|---|---|---|
| `migration`, `m` | Migration (forward change) | `MigrationItemType.Migration` | `MigrationItemType.MigrationSettings` |
| `breaking`, `b` | Breaking (contract phase) | `MigrationItemType.Breaking` | `MigrationItemType.BreakingSettings` |

- `<name>`: free text, informational only (stored in the database). For a script with an explicit type it is the third part; without a type it is the second part; for a settings file it is the optional fourth part. Further dot-separated parts are ignored.
- If the second part of a `.sql` file is not a type token, the file is a Migration and the second part is its name: `20260808104925.create-users-table.sql` is Migration, name `create-users-table`. A name that equals a type token (`m`, `b`, `migration`, `breaking`) is read as the type. `settings`/`s` is not a type token in a `.sql` name (`005.settings.sql` is a Migration named `settings`).
- `undo` and `u` are reserved: DbLive has no undo scripts (Section 18.8). A file whose second part is `undo` or `u`, with any extension (`005.undo.sql`, `005.u.sql`, `005.undo.settings.json`, `005.u.s.json`), fails the deployment before anything runs with `UndoNotSupportedException`, which names the file: delete it. It is not read as a migration named `undo`, which would undo its own version. A third part `undo` is only a name (`005.migration.undo.sql` is a Migration named `undo`).
- A settings file belongs to one script and needs that script: `<version>.breaking.settings.json` without a breaking script of that version is an error. Settings files of one version do not inherit from each other (Section 9.3).

Examples:

```
001.migration.sql                       Migration v1
002.m.orders.sql                        Migration v2, name "orders"
002.b.sql                               Breaking v2
004.migration.settings.json             settings of Migration v4
004.m.s.json                            the same, short form (only one of the two may exist)
005.b.s.json                            settings of Breaking v5
20260808104925.create-users-table.sql   Migration v20260808104925
20260808104925.migration.settings.json  settings of that migration (any migration file name)
```

Errors raised while reading the project:

| Situation | Exception |
|---|---|
| Version part is not digits only (also `+001.migration.sql`, `config.json`, `readme.sql`, a macOS `._001.migration.sql`) | `InvalidMigrationVersionException` |
| Old per-version settings file `<version>.settings.json` / `<version>.s.json` | `ObsoleteMigrationSettingsFileException` (message names the new file) |
| Other `.json` file in Migrations (`004.custom.json`, `004.migration.json`) | `UnknownMigrationSettingsException` |
| An undo script or its settings file (`005.undo.sql`, `005.u.sql`, `005.undo.settings.json`) | `UndoNotSupportedException` (message names the file) |
| Two files with the same version and type (also `001.migration.sql` + `1.m.sql`, `004.m.s.json` + `004.migration.settings.json`) | `DuplicateMigrationItemException` |
| A version has breaking/settings but no migration file | `MigrationItemMustExistsException` |
| A settings file without its script (`004.b.s.json` without a breaking script) | `MigrationSettingsWithoutScriptException` |
| A settings file with an unknown key (also the old `MigrationTimeout`), invalid JSON, or `"TransactionWrapLevel": "Deployment"` | `InvalidMigrationItemSettingsException` (message names the file) |
| `EnforceTimestampVersion: true` and the version is not `yyyyMMddHHmmss` (14 digits, valid date, year from 2000 to next month's year) | `InvalidMigrationVersionException` |

Version strategy: sequential numbers (`001`, `002`) are fine for one developer. For teams, use timestamps (`yyyyMMddHHmmss`, UTC) and set `"EnforceTimestampVersion": true` to avoid collisions between branches.

### 5.2 Which migrations are applied

- A version is pending when its Migration item is not `applied` in `dblive.migration`.
- All pending versions are applied in ascending version order, **including versions lower than the highest applied one** (a branch merged later with an older timestamp still gets applied). There is no "out of order" check.
- Subfolders are irrelevant to matching: items are matched by `(version, type)`, so moving old migrations into `Migrations/Old/` is safe.
- At the start of every deployment, all migration items found in the project are recorded in `dblive.migration` (status `none`) before anything runs. Items that are not applied yet are updated in place when their file changes. Only the hash is stored, not the content: the project is the source of the scripts. Rows of items deleted from the project stay; nothing runs them, because the migration and breaking phases and the checksum validation take the scripts and their settings from the project.
- **The project must have every version applied to the database.** At the start of every deployment (whatever the `DeployParameters`, also a `Breaking` run), after the self-deployment and before the checksum validation (Section 12), DbLive compares the applied versions with the project. Applied versions the project lacks → `DatabaseAheadOfProjectException` (`Versions`: those versions, ascending): no migration row is written and no script of the project runs. Causes: an older build is deployed (DbLive does not roll back a database: roll back the application and keep the database, Section 18.8), or migration files were deleted from the project (restore them). A version whose Migration item was recorded but never applied (a failed migration) does not count.

### 5.3 Execution of a migration version

Rule: each item (migration, breaking) is one unit: its own transaction, by its own settings (Section 9.3). After any item the database is consistent at the version level, so a deployment may stop between items and continue later.

For each pending version, in order:
1. Effective settings of the Migration item = `<version>.migration.settings.json` (if present) over the project `settings.json`, key by key.
2. Open a transaction with the effective `TransactionIsolationLevel` and `Timeout` if the effective `TransactionWrapLevel` is `Migration` (default). With `None`, no transaction. With project-level `Deployment`, the item runs inside the deployment transaction (an item `None` then logs a warning and has no effect).
3. Execute the Migration item; the SQL command gets the same isolation level (without a transaction it is set on the connection, Section 9.3) and the same `Timeout`. Mark it `applied`.
4. Commit.

The migration script and its status update are committed together. If a migration fails, the deployment stops with `MigrationDeploymentException` (the message names the file and contains the SQL error, or the cause of an error that does not come from the server, such as a command timeout; the inner exception is the `DbLiveSqlException`); earlier versions stay committed (with the default `Migration` level). A failed item is not marked `applied`, so the next deployment runs the **whole** script again: an item with `TransactionWrapLevel: None` must be re-runnable (`if not exists`, `drop ... if exists`, `create index concurrently if not exists` with a BeforeDeploy script that drops the index if it is invalid, Section 18.7).

The `[SqlDeployFact]` deployment test runs the breaking script of every migration once, as production does (Section 13.3): it does not test that a script with `TransactionWrapLevel: None` that failed halfway can run again.

### 5.4 Checksums

Before anything is deployed, every **applied** item (migration, breaking) is compared with the project file by `(version, type)`:
- Hash: XxHash64 of the file text (UTF-8) with CRLF replaced by LF. Any change, including whitespace and comments, is a mismatch; CRLF/LF line endings are not.
- `MigrationChecksumMode: "Strict"` (default): throws `MigrationChecksumMismatchException` listing the files.
- `MigrationChecksumMode: "Warn"`: logs a warning per file and continues.
- `DeployParameters.RepairMigrationChecksums = true`: overwrites the stored hashes with the current file hashes and continues. Use only when the database already matches the files (for example after a comment-only edit).
- Items not applied yet (for example the breaking script of a version whose breaking phase has not run) can be edited freely; the new hash is saved.
- Settings items are never checksum-validated.

Line endings: a Windows checkout (CRLF, `core.autocrlf=true`) and a Linux checkout (LF) of the same file have the same hash, so one database can be deployed from both; no `.gitattributes` is needed. Only CRLF is normalized: a lone CR or a Unicode line separator is a change. Scripts run with the line endings of the file. Migration hashes stored by DbLive versions that hashed the raw text still match the same file with either line endings; they are not rewritten. A code file is compared with the current hash only: a code file that DbLive 1.x deployed from a CRLF checkout runs once more on the first deployment with DbLive 2.0, and its row gets the current hash.

### 5.5 Breaking phase and breaking items of migrations

The breaking phase runs only when `DeployParameters.DeployBreaking = true`, after migrations and code, in this order:

1. **Guard.** Every code file of the project (Section 6) must have an `applied` row in `dblive.code` with its current content hash: the normal deployment of this build completed. Otherwise the deployment fails with `CodeNotDeployedException` (`Count`: how many code files differ; `RelativePaths`: the first 5 by path; the message names them and says to deploy with `DeployParameters.Default` first) and no breaking script runs, neither of the Code folder nor of migrations. The check is the one the code deployer uses to skip a file (`[hash match]`). A run that also deploys code (`DeployCode = true`) stops at a failed code file before the breaking phase, so the guard always passes there; a project without code files always passes. It catches the breaking stage of build N+1 started although its `Default` run failed in the code phase (migrations of N+1 committed, then a code file failed). Only code files are checked: a `Default` run that failed earlier (in BeforeDeploy, or in a migration after the migrations before it were committed) or did not run is caught only when build N+1 added or changed a code file. When it did not, the guard passes, and the breaking phase runs every breaking script of the Code folder and the breaking scripts of the migrations that are applied. DbLive does not guard against this operator mistake: never start the breaking phase unless the `Default` run of the same build succeeded. It does not check that the release is still the current one: after a rollback of the application the code of N+1 stays deployed, and after a later release that brought deleted code files back (a `git revert`, or the previous build of a code-only release) every code file of N+1 can still match. Never start the breaking phase of a release that was rolled back or replaced (Section 18.8).
2. **Breaking scripts of the Code folder**, all of them, every time (Section 6.1).
3. **Breaking items of migrations**, below.

Breaking items of migrations:
- Applied for every version whose Migration item is `applied` and whose Breaking item is not `applied`, in version order. A breaking script of a version whose migration has not been applied is never run.
- Each breaking script runs **in its own transaction** (version by version), by `<version>.breaking.settings.json` over the project settings. The migration's settings file is not used for the breaking script. If one fails, the breaking scripts of lower versions stay applied.
- Once applied, a breaking file is checksum-protected like a migration.
- When none is pending, the log says `No migration breaking scripts to apply.`

---

## 6. Code objects

- Every `*.sql` under `Code/` that does not match `TestFilePatterns`, is not a breaking script (Section 6.1) and is not `setup.test.sql` is a code item, identified by its relative path, ignoring case (for example `Code/dbo/GetUser.sql`).
- A code item is executed when no `applied` record with the same relative path and content hash exists in `dblive.code`. Unchanged files are skipped (logged as `[hash match]`).
- A changed, moved or renamed file is executed again. A rename that changes only case (`GetUser.sql` to `getUser.sql`, `Code` to `code`) keeps the identity of the file, so it is not executed again. **DbLive never drops code objects** (DBAs may create objects outside DbLive). A procedure removed from the repository stays in the database until a breaking script drops it.
- A deleted file: every deployment with `DeployCode = true`, after the code deployed successfully, sets `status = 'removed'` (and `verified_utc` = now) on the `dblive.code` rows whose file is neither a code file nor a breaking script of the Code folder of the project. The object stays. If the file comes back, its row is not `applied`, so it is executed again and the object is restored: a file brought back by a later release (`git revert` of its deletion) runs again even if its content did not change, because the breaking phase may have dropped its object in between. Without a `ProjectId` (Section 14), two projects deployed to one database mark each other's rows, and the other project redeploys all its code on its next deployment (slower, harmless).
- Manual changes made directly in the database are not detected: the file hash still matches, so the file is not re-run. To force a redeploy, change the file, or delete its row from `dblive.code` (`delete from dblive.code where relative_path = lower('Code/dbo/GetUser.sql');`).
- Execution order: groups listed in `CodeSubFoldersDeploymentOrder` (in that order), then everything else. Inside a group, up to `NumberOfThreadsForCodeDeploy` (10) files run in parallel. A failed file goes to the end of the queue and is retried up to `MaxCodeDeployRetries` (5) attempts in total. This resolves most dependency orders (a view that uses a function deployed later succeeds on retry). After the last attempt: `CodeDeploymentAggregateException`. Exception: with `TransactionWrapLevel: Deployment` a file whose error ended the deployment transaction is not retried, and the deployment fails at once with the error of the file (`Deploy code file error. File path: <path>. The error ended the deployment transaction, so the file is not retried.`). On SQL Server most errors leave the transaction open, but it is rolled back by any run-time error with `XACT_ABORT ON` (a missing dependency included), by a failed conversion and by a deadlock. `set xact_abort on` applies to the rest of the file that runs it (all its `GO` batches), not to the scripts after it: each script gets a reset session. On PostgreSQL every error aborts the transaction, but in the deployment transaction each code file runs under a savepoint (`dblive_code_item`): after an error DbLive rolls back to it, which undoes the statements of the failed attempt and makes the transaction usable again, so files are retried as without a transaction. On both providers the transaction also ends when the connection breaks (an error of severity 20 or more on SQL Server, a terminated session) or `DeploymentTimeout` passes; that file is not retried either. Order the dependencies that such errors hit with `CodeSubFoldersDeploymentOrder`, and on SQL Server leave `set xact_abort on` out of code files.
- Put objects other code depends on, such as schemas and types, in a group listed first: `"CodeSubFoldersDeploymentOrder": ["schemas"]`.
- `CodeSubFoldersDeploymentOrder` entries are folder paths relative to `Code`, matched as path prefixes (case-insensitive). Nested entries may use `/` or `\`: `"dbo/functions"` and `"dbo\\functions"` work on any OS. An entry that matches no code files logs a warning and forms an empty group.
- Code items are not wrapped in a transaction (each file is its own command) unless `TransactionWrapLevel` is `Deployment`, in which case code deploys single-threaded inside the deployment transaction. When an error ends that transaction (some errors on SQL Server, a broken connection, the deployment timeout: see the retries above), the file is not retried: order the dependencies with `CodeSubFoldersDeploymentOrder`. On PostgreSQL a file with several statements runs as one implicit transaction, so it fails or succeeds as a whole (Section 16); in the deployment transaction the rollback to its savepoint does the same. Each such savepoint of a file that changes something is a subtransaction: a deployment transaction with more than 64 of them (attempts of code files count) overflows the subtransaction cache of its session, and while it runs, other sessions check row visibility through `pg_subtrans`, a known slowdown of a busy server and its replicas.
- Per-file command timeout: `CodeItemTimeout` (30 seconds by default); on SQL Server it applies to each `GO` batch of the file.
- One file can create several objects. SQL Server: separate batches with `GO`. Keep one logical object per file so that redeploys stay small.

Versioned interface pattern (zero downtime): keep one file per logical object and rename the object when its contract changes (`GetUsers_v1` becomes `GetUsers_v2` in the same file). The old version stays in the database for old application instances; drop it later in a breaking script next to the file (Section 6.1). To bring `GetUsers_v1` back as the current version, revert the file in git and deploy a new release: its hash differs, so it runs again; `GetUsers_v2` stays (Section 18.8).

SQL Server code file:

```sql
create or alter proc dbo.GetUser_v2
    @UserId int
as
    select UserId, Name
    from dbo.Users
    where UserId = @UserId
go
```

PostgreSQL code file (`create or replace` cannot change a function's return type, so drop first when the signature changes):

```sql
drop function if exists get_customer_total_spent(int);

create function get_customer_total_spent(p_customer_id int)
returns numeric(12,2)
language plpgsql
as
$$
begin
    return (select coalesce(sum(i.total), 0) from invoice i where i.customer_id = p_customer_id);
end;
$$;
```

### 6.1 Breaking scripts of the Code folder

Drop old versions of code objects here, next to the code they clean up. A code-only release needs no migration.

```
Code/dbo/GetUser.sql             create or alter proc dbo.GetUser_v2 ... (was GetUser_v1)
Code/dbo/GetUser.breaking.sql    drop proc if exists dbo.GetUser_v1;
```

- Names (ignoring case, any subfolder of `Code/`): `<name>.breaking.sql` next to `<name>.sql`, or `breaking.sql` for its folder; short forms `<name>.b.sql`, `b.sql`. The pair is a naming convention only: DbLive does not link a breaking script to a code file, so a breaking script without a code file is valid (a procedure retired together with its file).
- Never deployed as code, never a test. A name that also matches `TestFilePatterns` → `BreakingScriptMatchesTestPatternException` (Section 4).
- Run in the breaking phase (`DeployBreaking = true`) after the guard and **before** the breaking items of migrations (Section 5.5), so dependents are dropped first: on PostgreSQL a view `_v1` blocks the `drop column` of a migration breaking script. Order: by relative path, ordinal, ignoring case.
- **No state: every script runs on every breaking deployment**, like AfterDeploy runs on every deployment. They must be idempotent (`drop ... if exists`): on a new database `_v1` never existed. A second run must not change the schema either: a condition checked on an object the script itself drops later (`if object_id('dbo.GetUser_v1') is null alter table ... drop column ...; drop proc if exists dbo.GetUser_v1;`) makes the second run drop more. `[SqlDeployFact]` runs every script a second time and compares the schema (Section 13.3). A failure in the middle of a script leaves some old objects dropped and others not (on PostgreSQL a multi-statement file is one implicit transaction and is rolled back as a whole); the next breaking deployment finishes the job. Without state a revert keeps working: N+1 breaking drops `_v1` → N+2 reverts the code file and deletes the breaking script (`_v1` is back) → a later release that brings the breaking script back drops `_v1` again in its breaking deployment.
- Execution: each file is one command without its own transaction, like a code file (inside the deployment transaction with `TransactionWrapLevel: Deployment`), isolation level `TransactionIsolationLevel`, timeout `CodeItemTimeout`. No item settings files. A failed script stops the deployment with `CodeDeploymentException` (message names the file, inner exception holds the SQL error); the scripts after it do not run.
- Each run writes the file's row in `dblive.code`: `item_type = 'breaking'`, `status` `applied` or `error` (with `error`), `content_hash`, `applied_utc` (time of the last run), `execution_time_ms`. A deployment of a build without the file marks its row `removed` and sets `verified_utc` (Section 6); a later run does not clear `verified_utc`. Failed ones: `select relative_path, error from dblive.code where status = 'error';`. With `TransactionWrapLevel: Deployment` a failed deployment is rolled back and leaves no `error` row (code files too): the error is in the exception and the log.
- No checksum protection. Code is deployed by state: to bring an old version of an object back, revert its file in git and deploy a new release (Section 18.8).
- Old version in a file of its own (`GetUser_v1.sql`) that build N+1 deletes: put `drop proc if exists dbo.GetUser_v1;` into `GetUser_v1.breaking.sql` (no code file next to it). N+1 marks the row of `GetUser_v1.sql` `removed` (Section 6), so a later release that brings the file back executes it again and restores `GetUser_v1`.
- Before this feature a code-only release needed a new migration version with a trivial migration (`select 1;`) only to carry the drop in its breaking script. Do not create such versions any more.

---

## 7. BeforeDeploy and AfterDeploy

- `BeforeDeploy/*.sql` runs after the migration items are recorded and before migrations; `AfterDeploy/*.sql` runs after the breaking step.
- They run on **every** deployment, whatever the `DeployParameters` flags (also with the `Breaking` preset). Nothing is skipped by hash; `dblive.folder_items` only records the last run.
- Order: by relative path, ordinal, ignoring case (`BeforeDeploy/01.sql`, `BeforeDeploy/02.sql`, `BeforeDeploy/sub/01.sql`); subfolders are included. Number the files to control the order.
- Not wrapped in a transaction (unless `TransactionWrapLevel` is `Deployment`). Command timeout: `BeforeDeployFolderTimeout` / `AfterDeployFolderTimeout` (6 hours).
- A failed script stops the deployment with `FolderDeploymentException` (Section 17): the message names the file and contains the SQL error. The scripts after it do not run; the scripts before it stay applied (without the deployment transaction). `dblive.folder_items` records only a run that succeeded.
- The database can be empty when BeforeDeploy runs (first deployment).
- Use them for idempotent maintenance: permissions, refreshing reference data with `merge`, enabling database options, statistics.
- Not a place for breaking changes such as dropping an old procedure version: AfterDeploy also runs with `DeployParameters.Default`, before the old application is gone. Use a breaking script of the Code folder (Section 6.1), which runs on every breaking deployment only.
- Only the folder names `BeforeDeploy` and `AfterDeploy` (or the names set by `BeforeDeployFolder` / `AfterDeployFolder`) are run. Another folder in the scripts root, for example `PostDeployment`, fails the deployment with `FilesOutsideProjectFoldersException` (Section 4).

---

## 8. SQL tests

### 8.1 Discovery

- `Tests/` and all of its subfolders: every `*.sql` except `setup.test.sql` is a test. Names do not matter.
- `Code/` and all of its subfolders: only files matching `TestFilePatterns`, except `setup.test.sql`. Convention: put `GetUser.test.sql` next to `GetUser.sql`. A test file must not also be named like a breaking script (`test.breaking.sql`, `t.b.sql`): `BreakingScriptMatchesTestPatternException` (Section 4).
- `setup.test.sql` in a folder (in `Tests/` or `Code/`) runs before **each** test in that same folder, in the same transaction. It is not inherited by subfolders.
- A test is identified by its relative path, ignoring case (for example `Tests/Orders/select-order.test.sql`).

### 8.2 Execution

For each test:
1. Open a transaction with `TestsTransactionIsolationLevel` (default `Serializable`) and timeout `UnitTestItemTimeout` (1 minute).
2. Execute `setup.test.sql` of the folder, if any (SQL Server: `GO` allowed).
3. Execute the test script and collect all result sets (SQL Server: **no `GO`**, the whole file is one batch).
4. Evaluate the assertion (8.3).
5. **Always roll back.** Tests leave no data behind and can be re-run.

`setup.test.sql` and the test run on separate connections inside the same transaction. Data changes made by `setup.test.sql` are visible to the test; session state is not (temporary tables, variables, `SET` options). Use permanent tables in `setup.test.sql`. If the setup file fails, the test fails with `ERROR: Setup file error. ...`. A test or setup file that runs longer than `UnitTestItemTimeout` fails with the provider's timeout error in `ErrorMessage` (`Execution Timeout Expired` on SQL Server, `Timeout during reading attempt` on PostgreSQL).

`DeployAsync` does not run the tests. They run in xUnit: `[SqlFact]` one by one (`RunTestAsync`), `[SqlDeployFact]` all of them after the release and after the breaking phase (Section 13). `IDbLiveTester.RunAllTestsAsync()` runs all of them against a deployed database, `NumberOfThreadsForTestsRun` (10) at a time. `[SqlDeployFact]` calls it; call it directly only without xUnit v2 (NUnit, MSTest, xUnit v3: one test that runs all SQL tests) or to test a database that is already deployed. It does not deploy:

```csharp
DbLiveBuilder builder = new DbLiveBuilder()
    .SqlServer()
    .SetDbConnection(connectionString)
    .SetProject(typeof(MyDbMarker).Assembly);

await builder.CreateDeployer().DeployAsync(DeployParameters.Default);   // leave out for a database that is already deployed
await builder.CreateTester().RunAllTestsAsync();   // never in a production deployer
```

A test database without xUnit. DbLive does not drop it: only the xUnit fixtures do (Section 13).
- In Docker: a container fixture builder (Section 11.5) gives a new database, `DbLiveBuilder builder = await new MsSqlContainerFixtureBuilder(typeof(MyDbMarker).Assembly).GetBuilderAsync();`, then `DeployAsync(DeployParameters.Default with { CreateDbIfNotExists = true })` (the database does not exist yet) and `RunAllTestsAsync()`. Nothing to drop: the container goes away when the test process ends.
- On a server of your own: a database with a fixed name (`MyDb_Tests`), dropped with your own SQL **before** the deployment, so that every run deploys the whole project to an empty database. A database kept between runs gets an incremental deployment, and the deployment is not tested in full. Before and not after: a run that fails before its end leaves the database, and the next run drops it anyway. `MsSqlFixtureBuilder` and `PostgreSqlFixtureBuilder` do not fit here: every call names a new database, which nothing drops without xUnit.

```csharp
using DbLive;
using DbLive.MSSQL;
using Microsoft.Data.SqlClient;   // comes with DbLive.MSSQL

const string connectionString = "Server=localhost;Database=MyDb_Tests;Trusted_Connection=True;TrustServerCertificate=True;";

await using (SqlConnection master = new(connectionString.SetMsSqlDatabaseName("master")))
{
    await master.OpenAsync();
    await using SqlCommand drop = new("""
        if db_id('MyDb_Tests') is not null
        begin
            alter database [MyDb_Tests] set single_user with rollback immediate;
            drop database [MyDb_Tests];
        end
        """, master);
    await drop.ExecuteNonQueryAsync();
}
SqlConnection.ClearPool(new SqlConnection(connectionString));

await using DbLiveBuilder builder = new DbLiveBuilder()
    .SqlServer()
    .SetDbConnection(connectionString)
    .SetProject(typeof(MyDbMarker).Assembly);

await builder.CreateDeployer().DeployAsync(DeployParameters.Default with { CreateDbIfNotExists = true });
await builder.CreateTester().RunAllTestsAsync();
```

PostgreSQL 13 or later: `NpgsqlConnection` (namespace `Npgsql`, comes with `DbLive.PostgreSQL`) on `connectionString.SetPostgreSqlDatabaseName("postgres")`, the SQL `drop database if exists mydb_tests with (force);`, then `NpgsqlConnection.ClearPool(new NpgsqlConnection(connectionString))`. A plain `drop database` fails while the database is in use, and the connections of DbLive stay in the connection pool: `single_user with rollback immediate` and `with (force)` close them. `ClearPool` removes the closed connections from the pool of the test database: without it a second run in the same process fails on PostgreSQL with `57P01: terminating connection due to administrator command`. Not `ClearAllPools`: it also clears the pools of other tests in the process, and their next connection in a `TransactionScope` on SQL Server fails with "Implicit distributed transactions have not been enabled". Verified on both providers with a second run after a deployment and a test run in the same process.

Before the first test it checks the database, and runs no test if a check fails:
- the database exists, otherwise `DatabaseNotFoundException` (Section 17);
- the DbLive tables exist, otherwise `DatabaseNotDeployedException` (namespace `DbLive.Testing`): the project was never deployed there, or the connection string points to another database;
- the database does not require a newer DbLive, otherwise `DatabaseRequiresNewerDbLiveException` (Section 15); the check only reads, a deployment stores the requirement;
- the ProjectId, compare only (Section 14): with a `ProjectId` in `settings.json`, a database with another value or with none fails with `ProjectIdMismatchException`;
- `TestsTransactionIsolationLevel` and `TransactionIsolationLevel` are supported by the provider, as at the start of a deployment.

Each result is stored in `dblive.unit_test_run`. If any test fails, `RunAllTestsAsync` throws `DbLive.Testing.UnitTestsFailedException` ("Unit test run failed. Failed test count X of Y.") after all tests have run. Its properties: `FailedCount`, `TotalCount`, and `FailedTests` (relative paths of the failed test files, sorted). Unhandled, it fails the calling test and gives a console app a non-zero exit code. The deployment was a separate call and stays committed: a failed test reports a bad release, the release stays deployed.

Parallel tests with `Serializable` isolation that touch the same tables can deadlock. If they do, set `"NumberOfThreadsForTestsRun": 1` or `"TestsTransactionIsolationLevel": "ReadCommitted"`.

### 8.3 Assertions: exact semantics

The test script returns result sets. One of them may be the **assert result set**: a result set whose first column is named `assert` (case-insensitive). Its first row holds the assertion type; an assert result set without rows fails the test.

```
[actual result sets ...]   select ... assert ...   [expected result sets ...]
```

- Result sets before the assert result set are **actual**; result sets after it are **expected**.
- At most one assert result set is allowed; a second one makes the test fail.
- Statements that return no result set (insert, update without `output`, `set`, `declare`) are ignored.
- Without an assert result set, the test passes if the script runs without an error. Raise an error for custom checks: `throw 50000, 'message', 0;` (SQL Server); on PostgreSQL `raise` works only in PL/pgSQL, so wrap it in a `do` block: `do $$ begin if (select count(*) from users) = 0 then raise exception 'message'; end if; end $$;`.
- Typo guard: when there is no assert result set, but some result set's first column has no name (SQL Server `''`, PostgreSQL `?column?`) or is within two edits of `assert` (`asstert`, `asert`, `Assret`), and its first value is a valid assert value, the test fails: `A result set with the value 'row-count=3' looks like an assert result set, but its first column is named 'asstert' instead of 'assert', so the test has no assertion. Rename the column, for example: select 'row-count=3' as assert.` A test without an assert whose act returns an unnamed string column with a value such as `empty` or `rows` trips this guard too; give that column an alias.

| Assert value | Passes when |
|---|---|
| `rows` | There are as many actual result sets as expected ones (at least one), and for each expected result set *i*: actual result set *i* has the same column count and the same column names (case-sensitive, same order), the same number of rows, and for each row *j* equal values. |
| `rows-with-schema` | Like `rows`, and the column SQL types are equal too (for example `nvarchar(255)`, `decimal(10, 2)`, `datetime2(7)` on SQL Server; `integer`, `bigint`, `numeric(12,2)`, `text`, `varchar(200)`, `timestamptz` on PostgreSQL). |
| `has-rows` | The first actual result set has at least one row. |
| `row-count=N` | There is exactly one actual result set and it has exactly N rows. |
| `empty` | Same as `row-count=0`. |
| `single-row` | Same as `row-count=1`. |

Assert values are case-insensitive, and spaces around them and around `=` are ignored (`Row-Count = 3` works). An unknown value fails the test with a list of supported values; `row-count` without a number (`row-count`, `row-count=abc`) fails with `Please use row-count=[Number] to assert row count. Example: row-count=10.`

Value comparison in `rows`: each value is serialized to JSON and the strings are compared.
- `int` 10 equals `bigint` 10. `decimal` 150.00 does **not** equal `int` 150 or `decimal` 150.0; the scale must match. Cast expected values: `cast(150 as decimal(10,2))`.
- Strings are compared exactly (case- and whitespace-sensitive).
- Dates: compare dates with dates of the same type. A date serializes as `"2026-01-01T00:00:00"`, so `'2026-01-01'` never equals it; cast the expected value to the column's type: `cast('2026-01-01' as date)`. On PostgreSQL a `timestamptz` value is read as UTC (`...Z`), so it equals only a `timestamptz`: `cast('2026-01-01 00:00:00+00' as timestamptz)`.
- `NULL` equals `NULL`.
- Column names must match exactly. SQL Server gives unnamed expressions an empty name, so `select dbo.F(1)` against `select cast('x' as nvarchar(10))` compares fine. PostgreSQL names them (`?column?`, or the function name), so alias both sides explicitly.
- Row order matters. Make the act deterministic (`order by`).
- Counts are checked before values: `Expected 2 result set(s), but 1 received.`, then per result set the columns, then `Expected 1 row(s), but 3 received.`, then the values. With several expected result sets the message starts with `Result set N:`. No result set after the assert result set: `No expected result set after the 'assert' result set.`
- Every result set returned before the assert result set is actual, including output from the Arrange part (`update ... output`, a `select` used for debugging). Remove such output, or move data setup into `setup.test.sql`, whose result sets are ignored.

### 8.4 Examples

SQL Server, exact values:

```sql
-- Arrange
set identity_insert dbo.Users on;
insert into dbo.Users (UserId, Name) values (10, 'TestUser10');

-- Act
exec dbo.GetUser_v2 @UserId = 10;

-- Assert
select assert = 'rows';
select 10 as UserId, 'TestUser10' as Name;
```

SQL Server, row count and types:

```sql
exec dbo.GetUser_v2 @UserId = -999;
select assert = 'row-count=0';
```

```sql
select dbo.GetFullName('first', 'last');
select assert = 'rows-with-schema';
select cast('first last' as nvarchar(255));
```

SQL Server, custom check:

```sql
declare @cnt int = (select count(*) from dbo.Users where Name = 'Admin');
if @cnt != 1 throw 50000, 'Expected one admin user.', 0;
```

Folder setup shared by several tests (`Tests/Orders/setup.test.sql` inserts three orders):

```sql
-- Tests/Orders/select-orders.test.sql
select OrderId from dbo.Orders;
select assert = 'row-count=3';
```

(`select count(*) ...` returns one row, so pairing it with `row-count=3` would fail. Count rows, not counts.)

PostgreSQL:

```sql
select * from get_album_summary(1);

select 'rows-with-schema' as assert;

select 1 as album_id
     , 'For Those About To Rock We Salute You' as album_title
     , 'AC/DC' as artist_name
     , cast(10 as bigint) as tracks_count
     , cast(10 as bigint) as sold_quantity
     , cast(9.90 as numeric) as total_amount
```

```sql
select * from genre;
select 'has-rows' as assert;
```

---

## 9. `settings.json`

### 9.1 Format

- Location: `Scripts/settings.json`. Optional; missing file means defaults.
- JSON with `//` and `/* */` comments allowed.
- **Property names are case-sensitive PascalCase** (`TransactionWrapLevel`, not `transactionWrapLevel`).
- **Unknown properties are errors** (`JsonException: The JSON property 'X' could not be mapped...`).
- **Trailing commas are errors.**
- Enum values are case-insensitive strings (`"none"`, `"None"`); numbers also work but are discouraged.
- `TimeSpan` format: `"hh:mm:ss"` or `"d.hh:mm:ss"` (for example `"01:00:00"`, `"1.00:00:00"`).
- List values replace the defaults; they are not merged.

### 9.2 All keys

| Key | Type | Default | Effect |
|---|---|---|---|
| `ProjectId` | string (max 128) | null | Binds the project to the database (Section 14). Not set: every deployment logs a warning. |
| `TransactionWrapLevel` | `Deployment` \| `Migration` \| `None` | `Migration` | Transaction scope (Section 10). Default for every migration and breaking script. |
| `TransactionIsolationLevel` | `ReadCommitted` \| `RepeatableRead` \| `Serializable` \| `Snapshot` | `ReadCommitted` | Isolation for deployment transactions and for every deployment command (a command without a transaction, such as a code file or a BeforeDeploy/AfterDeploy script, gets it on its connection); default for every migration and breaking script. `Snapshot` is SQL Server only and needs `ALLOW_SNAPSHOT_ISOLATION ON`. |
| `TestsTransactionIsolationLevel` | same | `Serializable` | Isolation of test transactions. |
| `TestFilePatterns` | string[] | `["test.*.sql","t.*.sql","*.test.sql","*.t.sql"]` | Which files in `Code/` are tests (and excluded from code deployment). |
| `MigrationsFolder` | string | `Migrations` | Folder path relative to the scripts root (same for the other `*Folder` settings). |
| `CodeFolder` | string | `Code` | |
| `TestsFolder` | string | `Tests` | |
| `BeforeDeployFolder` | string | `BeforeDeploy` | |
| `AfterDeployFolder` | string | `AfterDeploy` | |
| `CodeSubFoldersDeploymentOrder` | string[] | `[]` | Code subfolders deployed first, in this order. |
| `EnforceTimestampVersion` | bool | `false` | Require `yyyyMMddHHmmss` migration versions. |
| `MigrationChecksumMode` | `Strict` \| `Warn` | `Strict` | Reaction to edited applied migrations. |
| `NumberOfThreadsForCodeDeploy` | int | `10` | Parallel code deployment. |
| `MaxCodeDeployRetries` | int | `5` | Attempts per code file. |
| `NumberOfThreadsForTestsRun` | int | `10` | Parallel tests of `IDbLiveTester.RunAllTestsAsync()`, also in `[SqlDeployFact]`. |
| `DeploymentTimeout` | TimeSpan | `1.00:00:00` | Transaction timeout with `TransactionWrapLevel: Deployment`. |
| `MigrationTimeout` | TimeSpan | `12:00:00` | Default `Timeout` of every migration and breaking script: its command timeout and its transaction timeout. |
| `CodeItemTimeout` | TimeSpan | `00:00:30` | Command timeout per code file and per breaking script of the Code folder. |
| `UnitTestItemTimeout` | TimeSpan | `00:01:00` | Command and transaction timeout per test. |
| `BeforeDeployFolderTimeout` | TimeSpan | `06:00:00` | Command timeout per BeforeDeploy file. |
| `AfterDeployFolderTimeout` | TimeSpan | `06:00:00` | Command timeout per AfterDeploy file. |

Folder settings and `CodeSubFoldersDeploymentOrder` entries are relative paths. Nested paths may use `/` or `\` on any OS: `"db/Code"` and `"db\\Code"` are the same folder. Leading and trailing separators are ignored.

Example:

```json
{
  // Binds this project to a database; max 128 characters.
  "ProjectId": "billing-prod",
  "TransactionWrapLevel": "Migration",
  "TransactionIsolationLevel": "ReadCommitted",
  "EnforceTimestampVersion": true,
  "MigrationChecksumMode": "Strict",
  "CodeSubFoldersDeploymentOrder": [ "schemas", "types" ]
}
```

### 9.3 Item settings (`<version>.<item>.settings.json`)

One optional settings file per script: `<version>.migration.settings.json`, `<version>.breaking.settings.json`. Short forms combine `m` / `b` with `s` / `settings`: `<version>.m.s.json`, `<version>.b.settings.json`, `<version>.breaking.s.json`. A settings file applies to its own script only and requires that script to exist (Section 5.1).

Same JSON rules as `settings.json` (Section 9.1). Allowed keys only:

| Key | Values | Effect for this script | Default when the key is missing |
|---|---|---|---|
| `TransactionWrapLevel` | `Migration` \| `None` | `Migration`: the script runs in its own transaction. `None`: no transaction (needed for online/concurrent index builds, `ALTER DATABASE`, full-text DDL, `CREATE/DROP INDEX CONCURRENTLY`, `VACUUM`; on PostgreSQL keep such a statement alone in its file, Section 16). `Deployment` is an error (`InvalidMigrationItemSettingsException`). | project `TransactionWrapLevel` |
| `TransactionIsolationLevel` | `ReadCommitted` \| `RepeatableRead` \| `Serializable` \| `Snapshot` | Isolation of the script's transaction and of its SQL command. Without a transaction (`None`) it is set on the connection: `SET TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL` on SQL Server, `SET SESSION CHARACTERISTICS AS TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL` on PostgreSQL (the level of the implicit transaction of the command). | project `TransactionIsolationLevel` |
| `Timeout` | TimeSpan | Timeout of the script's transaction **and** of its SQL command. | project `MigrationTimeout` |

- A missing key falls back to the **project** settings, never to another item's file: `004.migration.settings.json` does not affect `004.breaking.sql`.
- The old key `MigrationTimeout` is an unknown key → `InvalidMigrationItemSettingsException`. Rename it to `Timeout`.
- A `TransactionIsolationLevel` the provider does not support (`Snapshot` on PostgreSQL) fails the deployment when the project is loaded, before anything runs (Section 12, step 1): `NotSupportedTransactionIsolationLevelException`, whose message names the settings file.
- Project `TransactionWrapLevel: Deployment` + item `None`: a warning is logged, and the script runs inside the deployment transaction. With `Deployment` every script runs at the isolation level and under the `DeploymentTimeout` of the deployment transaction: an item's `TransactionIsolationLevel` is only validated, and its `Timeout` is only the command timeout.
- `None` is the author's guarantee that the database keeps working if the script stops midway. A failed script reruns from the start on the next deployment, so it must be re-runnable (`if not exists`, `drop ... if exists`).
- Settings files are read from the project on every deployment; the database stores only their hash.

```json
// 20260815120000.migration.settings.json: online index build, no long transaction
{
  "TransactionWrapLevel": "None",
  "Timeout": "01:00:00"
}
```

---

## 10. Transactions and timeouts

| `TransactionWrapLevel` (project) | Behavior |
|---|---|
| `Migration` (default) | Each migration and breaking script runs in its own transaction, by its item settings (Section 9.3). This applies to migrations, to the breaking step (one transaction per breaking script of a migration, in version order) and to both runs of a migration breaking script in `[SqlDeployFact]` (Section 5.3). Code, breaking scripts of the Code folder, BeforeDeploy and AfterDeploy are not transactional. |
| `Deployment` | The applied versions check, checksum validation, migration saving, BeforeDeploy, migrations, code (single-threaded), breaking and AfterDeploy run in one transaction (all or nothing). Item files cannot opt out (`None` → warning, runs inside). Use for small databases or test environments, not for 24/7 production. |
| `None` | No transactions, except self-deployment and tests. An item file with `"TransactionWrapLevel": "Migration"` still gets its own transaction. |

Always transactional: DbLive's own schema deployment (Serializable, 5 minutes), each test. There is no special transaction for the breaking phase: its scripts follow the item rules above.

**Transaction timeouts.** DbLive uses `System.Transactions.TransactionScope`. .NET caps every scope timeout at the process-wide `TransactionManager.MaximumTimeout` (10 minutes by default). Before opening a transaction, DbLive raises that cap to the transaction's timeout (it never lowers it), so `MigrationTimeout`, item `Timeout`, `DeploymentTimeout` and `UnitTestItemTimeout` apply as configured. Side effect: other `TransactionScope`s in the same process are afterwards capped at the largest timeout DbLive used, not at 10 minutes. A transaction that runs longer than its timeout is aborted with `TransactionAbortedException`.

Command timeouts (the `*Timeout` settings except `DeploymentTimeout`, which is a transaction timeout only, and item `Timeout`) are applied separately to each SQL command, in whole seconds; on SQL Server to each `GO` batch.

---

## 11. C# API

Namespaces: what a deployer calls is in `DbLive`: the builder and its methods, `IDbLive`, `DeployParameters`, `IDbLiveFixtureBuilder`, and the exceptions of Section 17 but three. The tests are in `DbLive.Testing` (`IDbLiveTester`, `TestRunResult`, `UnitTestsFailedException`, `DatabaseNotDeployedException`, and `SchemaChangedException` of the deployment test), the providers in `DbLive.MSSQL` and `DbLive.PostgreSQL`, the xUnit integration in `DbLive.xunit`. Every other type is internal (see [Versioning](https://zacoders.github.io/DbLive/versioning/)).

### 11.1 `DbLiveBuilder` (namespace `DbLive`)

```csharp
public sealed class DbLiveBuilder : IDisposable, IAsyncDisposable
{
    public IDbLive CreateDeployer();
    public IDbLiveTester CreateTester();    // DbLive.Testing: run all SQL tests, or one by relative path
}
```

Extension methods:

| Method | Package / namespace | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| `.SqlServer()` | `DbLive.MSSQL` | Use the SQL Server provider. |
| `.PostgreSQL()` | `DbLive.PostgreSQL` | Use the PostgreSQL provider. |
| `.SetDbConnection(string sqlDbConnectionString)` | `DbLive` | Target database. The database name in it is created when `CreateDbIfNotExists` is true. |
| `.SetProject(Assembly)` | `DbLive` | Read the scripts embedded in the SQL project assembly (Sections 3.1, 3.4). |
| `.SetScriptsFolder(string scriptsPath)` | `DbLive` | Read the scripts from a folder instead (Section 3.4). |
| `.LogToConsole()` | `DbLive` | Serilog console logger. |
| `.LogTo(Serilog.ILogger)` | `DbLive` | Any Serilog logger. The builder does not dispose it. |
| `.LogToXUnitOutput(ITestOutputHelper)` | `DbLive.xunit` | Log to xUnit test output. |

Exactly one provider, one connection and one project (`SetProject` or `SetScriptsFolder`) are required; when one of them is set twice, the last call wins. DbLive reads the scripts only from the SQL project assembly or a folder. Calling a configuration method after `Create*` creates the objects anew on the next `Create*` call. The builder has no other configuration: the dependency injection inside it is internal.

Connection string helpers (handy for tests):

```csharp
using DbLive.MSSQL;       // "…".SetMsSqlDatabaseName("X"), "…".SetRandomMsSqlDatabaseName() -> "DbLive--<guid>"
using DbLive.PostgreSQL;  // "…".SetPostgreSqlDatabaseName("x"), "…".SetRandomPostgreSqlDatabaseName() -> "dblive--<guid>"
```

### 11.2 `IDbLive`

```csharp
Task DeployAsync(DeployParameters parameters);
```

Deploys only. The SQL tests are not part of it (Section 8.2).

A SQL error of a script is a `DbLiveSqlException` (`SqlError` holds provider details: number, severity, line), the inner exception of the deployment errors of Section 17. `SqlError` is empty when the error does not come from the server: a command timeout, a lost connection. The message has the cause then: on PostgreSQL the distinct messages of the provider's exception chain, one per line, because Npgsql wraps the cause in `NpgsqlException` "Exception while reading from stream" (a command timeout: `Timeout during reading attempt`). The provider's exception is the inner exception.

DbLive's database access is internal: `DeployAsync` creates the database (`CreateDbIfNotExists`) and checks it, the xUnit fixtures drop theirs. Other SQL, also the drop of a test database without xUnit (Section 8.2), runs on a connection of your own (ADO.NET, Dapper) with the same connection string.
